question: When the avatar enters an unfamiliar game, how does it read the game's physics intent: faithful simulation it must respect, or exaggerated cartoon physics it can exploit
pole_low: reads physics as law, plays carefully inside it
pole_high: reads physics as a toy, probes for exploitable exaggeration
why: A physics-first avatar wastes its best moves in a cartoon game and dies stupidly in a simulation. Reading the intent early decides its whole risk posture. Axis drafted by MiniMax (fleet mining 2026-10-14), reframed by Muse toward avatar behaviour
evidence_needed: Maker and analyst transcripts where physics intent is discussed (Barji, Juniper Dev, Jack Sather), plus the avatar's own first-session logs once it plays

question: How visibly does a game teach its own rules in the first minutes, and how much must the avatar discover by experiment instead
pole_low: the game teaches explicitly, the avatar can trust instruction
pole_high: the game teaches nothing, every rule is an experiment
why: An avatar that experiments in a teaching game looks dumb; one that waits for instruction in a discovery game never moves. The detection changes its opening behaviour completely
evidence_needed: Design analyst transcripts on teaching without tutorials (Game Design Library, The Game Overanalyser) and maker devlogs on first-five-minutes design

question: How much failure information does the game itself hand back (explicit feedback, replays, stats) versus how much the avatar must reconstruct forensically
pole_low: the game explains every failure, the avatar just listens
pole_high: the game says nothing, the avatar must rebuild the cause itself
why: Decides whether the avatar's post-mortem move is a reading or an investigation, and how much of the debrief the coach can trust. Axis from MiniMax fleet mining, reframed by Muse
evidence_needed: Analyst transcripts on failure feedback design, plus Jesse Gillett style forensic segments as the high-pole behaviour model

question: How scarce is the game's core resource really, beneath its presentation: generous economy wearing a scarce costume, or true scarcity
pole_low: abundance in costume, the avatar can spend freely
pole_high: true scarcity, every spend is a commitment
why: Misreading scarcity is the classic new-player death. A maker-trained avatar audits drop rates and prices before it trusts the story the game tells about them
evidence_needed: Maker transcripts on economy design (Indie Game Clinic, CodyCantEatThis) and analyst economy breakdowns

question: How much of a game's experience is authored set pieces versus systems colliding, and where should the avatar expect the memorable moments to come from
pole_low: authored, the avatar plays the script well
pole_high: systemic, the avatar manufactures moments by colliding systems
why: The avatar performs differently in each world: precision in authored games, provocation in systemic ones. Pairs with spectacle-001 from the game side of the glass
evidence_needed: Design essays on emergence vs authorship (Jack Sather, Game Overanalyser), devlogs where a kept accident became the game (Juniper Dev, Zoteling)

question: How much difficulty control does the game hand the player (settings, assists, self-imposed rules), and should the avatar treat that as part of the game or as a coach-level decision
pole_low: difficulty is the game's, the avatar plays what is served
pole_high: difficulty is a player surface, the avatar and coach tune it openly
why: For a coached avatar this decides who owns challenge: the product's youngest users will reach for these levers, and the avatar needs a stance before they do. Axis from MiniMax fleet mining, reframed by Muse
evidence_needed: Analyst transcripts on accessibility and difficulty design (Indie Game Clinic), plus playtest evidence once the avatar has coach sessions
